summary: Updates the ODETTE File Transfer Protocol, used for exchanging business data between trading partners, to version 2. It adds secure authenticated communication using TLS, file encryption, signing, and compression via CMS, and signed receipts. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A safe way for companies to send each other business files and get a signed receipt.

questions: what is an eerp in oftp
subtitle: A business file-transfer protocol with signed receipts, now with TLS, CMS file security and compression.

tldr.problem: Trading partners need to exchange business files automatically and be told reliably that the final destination received them. Internet FTP is interactive and has no file acknowledgements, which the RFC says makes it a poor fit for mission-critical business data.
tldr.mechanism: ODETTE-FTP exchanges Virtual Files in five phases using a small set of commands, with a Speaker and Listener taking turns. Version 2 adds TLS session security, file signing, encryption and compression using CMS, and signed end-to-end receipts (EERP) or negative responses (NERP).
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 2204 (version 1.3 of the protocol). The IESG note says it is not a candidate for any level of Internet Standard and was published at the RFC Editor's discretion.

today: RFC 5024 is Informational and the IESG note says it is not a candidate for any Internet Standard. It obsoletes RFC 2204 and has been updated by RFC 8996.

sections.title: What ODETTE-FTP Is For
sections.content:
The ODETTE File Transfer Protocol (ODETTE-FTP) was defined in 1986 by an ODETTE working group to meet the electronic data interchange (EDI) needs of the European automotive industry. It lets business applications exchange files peer to peer, automatically, with a defined acknowledgement on successful receipt. The RFC stresses that it is not a variant of Internet FTP, which is interactive and lacks file acknowledgements.

This memo describes version 2, a development of version 1.4. New features include session level encryption, file level encryption, secure authentication, file compression, signed end-to-end responses (EERP) and signed negative responses (NERP), a maximum file size increased to 9 PB, a virtual file description and extended error codes. It works directly between peers or via a Value Added Network, and over TCP/IP, X.25 and ISDN networks.

ODETTE-FTP is modelled on the OSI reference model, spans levels 4 to 7, and offers a File Service to a User Monitor (generally an application).
sections.eli5: It is a reliable courier for company files. Unlike ordinary file sharing, the courier brings back proof that the package arrived.

sections.title: Virtual Files
sections.content:
Data always travels as a Virtual File, a standard representation that hides differences between systems. Mapping a local file to and from the virtual form is not defined by the RFC. A Virtual File is identified by a dataset name, a date stamp (CCYYMMDD) and a time stamp (HHMMSScccc, where the counter cccc runs 0001 to 9999). These are set by the originator, are mandatory and must not be changed by intermediate locations.

Four record formats exist: F (fixed), V (variable), U (unstructured stream) and T (text, ASCII with CR-LF line ends and at most 2048 characters per line). An interrupted transfer can be restarted: F and V files restart on record boundaries, while U and T files restart at an offset in 1K (1024 octet) blocks.
sections.eli5: Before a file is sent, it is put into a standard box with a label showing its name, date and time. Both sides know how to open that kind of box.

sections.title: Phases, Turns and Commands
sections.content:
A session has five phases: Start Session, Start File, Data Transfer, End File and End Session. After End File, a new Start File phase may follow or the session may end. The side that opened the connection is the Initiator and the other is the Responder. The Responder speaks first, sending the Ready Message (SSRM), and the two sides then exchange SSID commands. Afterwards the Initiator is the Speaker and the Responder is the Listener; the turn is passed with a Change Direction (CD) command or when the Listener asks for it in its End File answer (EFPA).

The Speaker sends SFID to start a file and the Listener answers SFPA (yes) or SFNA (no). Data then flows in DATA buffers, and the Speaker ends the file with EFID, answered by EFPA or EFNA. Only the Speaker may send file requests. The Speaker may end the session with ESID, but only after the Listener has just given up its turn.

Flow control uses credit. A credit limit is negotiated at session start (the SSIDCRED field) and is the number of buffers the Speaker may send before it must wait for a Set Credit (CDT) command. Sending with no credit left is a protocol error and aborts the session. On protocol errors the session ends and both locations return to the IDLE state; timers guard against hangs.
sections.eli5: Only one side talks at a time, like walkie-talkies. The talker says what file is coming, sends it in pieces, and the listener says when to send more.

sections.title: Commands, Buffers and Framing
sections.content:
Each Exchange Buffer holds exactly one command, which starts with a one-octet command identifier; commands and data are never mixed and commands cannot be compressed. The SSRM begins I followed by the text ODETTE FTP READY; SSID is X, SFID and the others have their own letters, for example DATA is D and CDT is C. The SSID carries the protocol release level, identification code, password, buffer size, send/receive capability, compression, restart and credit settings. Release level 5 means revision 2.0, and the lowest level offered by either side is chosen.

Each party has an identification code based on ISO 6523 with an ODETTE identifier, a four-digit international code designator, an organisation code of up to 14 characters and a 6-character computer subaddress.

In a DATA buffer, records are cut into subrecords, each preceded by a one-octet header: one bit for end of record, one bit for compression, and a 6-bit count, so a subrecord covers 0 to 63 octets. The older buffer compression repeats a single octet, and the RFC says file level compression essentially deprecates it.

Over TCP, which does not keep message boundaries, every buffer gets a 4-octet Stream Transmission Header with a 4-bit version (0001), 4 reserved flag bits and a 24-bit length. The length ranges from 5 to 100003, because the largest negotiable buffer is 99999 octets. X.25 does not need this header.
sections.eli5: Every message starts with a one-letter code saying what kind it is. Over the Internet, each message also gets a length tag so the receiver knows where one message stops and the next starts.

sections.title: Receipts and Authentication
sections.content:
An End to End Response (EERP) tells the originator that the Virtual File reached its final destination. It is mandatory and may be sent in the same or a later session. If the originator asked for a signed EERP in the SFID, the EERP should be signed, though the final destination may fall back to an unsigned one. An intermediate location that distributes a file must collect responses from all destinations before sending its own. A signed EERP cannot be combined with broadcast, because only one destination can sign. A NERP reports that a file could not be delivered or processed for a non-temporary reason.

After sending an EERP or NERP the Speaker must wait for a Ready To Receive (RTR), which acts as hop-by-hop flow control and has no end-to-end meaning.

Optional ODETTE-FTP Authentication works inside the protocol on any network. The Initiator sends SECD, the Responder replies with an AUCH challenge, which is a 20-byte random number encrypted in a CMS envelope with the Initiator's public key. The Initiator decrypts it and returns it in AURP. The roles then repeat in the other direction. Validating the response is the application's job and the RFC calls this validation extremely important.
sections.eli5: The receiver sends back a signed postcard saying the file arrived. To prove who you are, the other side locks a random number in a box only you can open, and you tell them what was inside.

sections.title: Security Options and Considerations
sections.content:
Security uses X.509 certificates. For session security, ODETTE-FTP is layered over TLS the same way as over TCP, with a TLS server when receiving calls and a TLS client when calling. The Responder listens on Registered Port 3305 (odette-ftp) for plain connections and 6619 (odette-ftps) for TLS. With TLS alone for confidentiality, only the Responder needs a certificate, so a hub can protect sessions without every partner having one.

File security is applied to the whole file, in this exact order: insert record length headers (V files only), sign, compress, encrypt, where steps 2 to 4 are each optional. Enveloping uses CMS content types SignedData, CompressedData and EnvelopedData; compression uses ZLIB by default. File encryption lets a file stay encrypted across intermediaries, but the protocol commands and file names remain visible. These steps should generally be done off line to avoid session time outs. V files need 2-byte record length headers because processing destroys the record structure.

Two cipher suites are mandatory: 01 (3DES EDE CBC with 3 keys, RSA PKCS1 1.5, SHA-1) and 02 (AES 256 CBC, RSA PKCS1 1.5, SHA-1). Others can be agreed bilaterally.

On risks: if no security options are agreed, the send and receive passwords travel in plain text. The RFC says this is acceptable over X.25 and ISDN but risky over insecure public networks such as the Internet. All, some or none of the security options may be used, and the RFC gives no recommendation, noting a performance trade-off for strong algorithms and legal implications of signing all files and acknowledgements.

Authentication proves identity but does not mean authorisation; the application decides whether a partner may connect or exchange files. Certificate processing can fail in many ways, such as an expired certificate or an unreachable CRL, and software should clearly tell the user. Because either side can open the outbound connection, only one party needs to allow incoming connections through its firewall.
sections.eli5:
You can lock the whole road to the receiver, or lock each parcel, or both. Locking the road hides everything; locking the parcel keeps it safe even if many helpers carry it along the way.

Proving who you are is not the same as being allowed in, and without the locks your password goes out in the open.
